title: System Integrity and Secure Boot
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of System Integrity and Secure Boot and identify key concepts from the supplied syllabus.
Use an appropriate read-only check or controlled example to demonstrate system integrity and secure boot.
Describe one common failure mode, safety consideration, or platform/version difference relevant to this topic.

content.intro: This lesson introduces system integrity and secure boot as part of linux security and system hardening. Begin with an observation you can safely repeat, then explain what the result tells you and what it does not prove.
content.why_it_matters: Apply defense in depth, least privilege, controlled exposure, trusted software, audit evidence, and incident response.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Security is a series of controls: minimize privileges and exposure, keep software trusted and patched, protect secrets, and preserve audit evidence.

items.title: Secure Boot concepts
items.text: Secure Boot concepts: Identify the concept’s role in the workflow, choose a read-only inspection first, and record the version or distribution details that could change the result.

items.title: Kernel and boot-chain integrity
items.text: Kernel and boot-chain integrity: Separate what the kernel provides from what a userspace tool or application contributes; inspect the matching official documentation for version-specific details.

items.title: Integrity verification
items.text: Integrity verification: Identify the concept’s role in the workflow, choose a read-only inspection first, and record the version or distribution details that could change the result.

items.text: Signed software and packages: Use the tool appropriate to the distribution, inspect proposed changes first, and note the package/runtime version that determines behavior.

items.title: Recovery and key-management considerations
items.text: Recovery and key-management considerations: A backup or rollback is useful only when its integrity and restoration procedure have been verified in a separate test location.

The in-page example shows reference output only; it does not execute Bash/Linux commands on the CodeLeaf server. Commands and output formats may vary by distribution and installed utility version.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First, state what you expect from the example. Run it in the intended environment, capture standard output and any error message, and inspect the exit status where meaningful. Then connect the observation to this lesson: System Integrity and Secure Boot. Do not infer more than the evidence supports.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake
content_blocks.text: A common mistake is to assume system integrity and secure boot behaves identically on every distribution, kernel, utility version, and administrative policy. Verify the installed tool and consult the matching manual before using the procedure elsewhere.

content_blocks.title: Safety and compatibility
content_blocks.text: This comparison does not install or remove packages; choose the tool for the actual distribution. For commands that edit files, manage services, change network/firewall state, partition disks, change permissions recursively, or alter boot settings, use an isolated VM, take a snapshot/backup, review the exact target, and prepare a recovery path before acting.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the command is missing, check whether the required package is installed and which distribution you are using. If access is denied, do not immediately escalate to root; confirm the target path, identity, and required permission. If the result differs, capture the command, output, version, and environment so the issue can be reproduced.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember the core relationship: Security is a series of controls: minimize privileges and exposure, keep software trusted and patched, protect secrets, and preserve audit evidence. The goal is to explain the observed result, test a boundary case, and record a limitation rather than memorize a command in isolation.

content.task: In an isolated Linux lab, investigate system integrity and secure boot. Use the guided example as a starting point, record the output/status, and test one boundary, failure, or distribution-specific case. Explain what you learned without changing a production system.
task_acceptance_criteria: The practical step is aligned to this lesson and uses synthetic inputs or a disposable environment.
The submission records expected and observed behavior, including an exit status or error when relevant.
One boundary case, failure path, or version/distribution difference is tested and explained.
Any potentially destructive command is previewed and kept out of production; the result can be reproduced.
hints: Start with read-only inspection and use the manual page for the installed command.
Change one variable at a time and preserve the exact output/error.
Record the distribution, kernel/utility version, privileges, and any assumptions that affect the result.
